Three situations stand out, and each has a reason.

**Third down, short and medium.** On third-and-3 to third-and-6, defenses played man on about 60%
of charted dropbacks in both charting eras, far more than on first down (about 25 to 36%).[^manshare] The
defense knows where the ball has to go: just past the line to gain. Man coverage contests the
throw at the sticks instead of rallying to tackle after a catch short of them. It also pairs
naturally with a blitz, and third down invites one: the offense almost has to throw, so the
defense can send extra rushers without much fear of a run, and a quick incompletion ends the
drive. Notice what happens on third-and-11 or more:
man coverage *drops* to its lowest rate of any situation. With that much to go, the defense is
happy to let the receiver catch the ball in front of it and tackle him short, which is a zone's
job. Third-and-long is the zone defense's down; third-and-medium is man's. And first down leans
zone for the opposite reason: the offense might run, or fake a run and throw, and man defenders
with their backs to the backfield are the worst-placed players on the field against both. Zone
defenders face the ball and can come up to tackle a runner.

**The red zone and the goal line.** As the field shrinks, man coverage takes over. Inside the
defense's 5-yard line, charters labelled 78 to 88% of dropbacks as man coverage, and Cover 0 on
41 to 62% of them, depending on the source. Near the goal line the biggest weakness of man
coverage nearly disappears. A receiver who beats his man deep runs out of field: the back line of
the end zone, the **end line**, acts like a safety that never misses. Zones, meanwhile, lose
their main tool: there is no depth to drop into, so zone defenders end up standing on the end
line while quick, sharp-breaking routes are completed in front of them. Man coverage contests the
catch itself. So defenses spend their deep defenders on the rush or on more man coverage. Read
the goal-line Cover 0 numbers with care, though: near the goal line "Cover 0" often means
"nobody deep, because there is no deep," not necessarily an all-out blitz. Of charted Cover 0
dropbacks inside the 5, only about 60 to 70% had five or more rushers.[^glzero] (The red zone gets its
own chapter: [Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).)

**Talent.** Man coverage is only as good as the worst matchup in it, so teams with great
cornerbacks play more of it. In nflverse charting, the Patriots played man on a larger share of
dropbacks than any other defense in 2018 and 2019 (about 61% and 68%), the seasons around Stephon
Gilmore's Defensive Player of the Year award; Miami, coached from 2019 to 2021 by Brian Flores, a
long-time Belichick assistant, led the league in 2020 and 2021; Denver, with Surtain, led it in
2024 and 2025.[^teamman] The reverse is true too. A defense with a weak link in the secondary, or
facing a quarterback who punishes defenders with their backs turned by running, leans toward zone,
where everyone faces the ball.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"NFL defenses are playing more and more man coverage."** You may see charts that say so. Be
careful. The public coverage labels come from two different charting sources (NGS through 2022,
FTN from 2023), and the man share jumps from about 29% of charted dropbacks in 2022 to about 44% in
2023 and 50% in 2024, then falls back to 31% in 2025. Defenses didn't change that much that fast;
the labelling did. Comparisons *within* a source (one season, or one era, as in the chart above)
are safe; trend lines across the 2022/2023 break are not. (The season-by-season figures are in the
note to the third-down paragraph above.)
:::

## How offenses attack man, and how the defense answers

Every offense has a list of plays it calls when it expects man coverage. You met most of them from
the offense's side in Part 4; here they are from the defense's side, paired with the counter each
one provokes. Notice that most of the defense's counters are things we've already met in this
chapter: the free defender, the banjo, the bracket.

| The offense's man-beater | Why it works against man | The defense's counter |
|---|---|---|
| **Crossers and mesh** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)) | A crossing receiver runs away from a trailing defender, through traffic. | A robber or rat sitting in the middle; defenders who pass crossers on to each other in combos. |
| **Rubs, stacks and bunches** | Defenders must go around receivers or teammates (the contact has to look incidental, or it is offensive pass interference). | Banjo and combo rules; pressing the front receiver of a stack to wreck the timing. |
| **The slant** ([The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)) | Beats an outside-leveraged defender inside, quickly. | Inside help: a rat or lurker under the slant; inside leverage in Cover 0. |
| **Double moves** | Punish a man defender who jumps the first break. | A deep safety over the top (Cover 1, a bracket); patient technique. |
| **Motion, especially at the snap** ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)) | Gives the receiver a running start and forces the defender to chase across the formation; it also reveals man. | Exchanges instead of travelling, so motion reveals less; zone calls disguised to look like man (and man calls disguised as zone). |
| **The running back on a linebacker** (the angle route) | The slowest cover man on the field is often matched on a quick back. | Putting a safety or a fast linebacker on the back; a free defender who helps on him. |
| **The scrambling quarterback** | Man defenders have their backs to him; nobody is left to tackle. | A spy, or a rat who keeps his eyes on the quarterback; more zone. |
| **The back-shoulder and the fade** | Against press, the ball is thrown where only the receiver can reach it. | A safety over the top; a cornerback who plays the receiver's hands (the out-of-phase technique above). |

The Chiefs' "Corn Dog" touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII, which you met in
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), are the
textbook case of the motion line in that table: the man defender went with the first move, the
receiver came back the other way, and nobody was there. The general lesson is the one you started
the chapter with. Man coverage asks each defender to *stay with a person*, and every man-beater is
a way of making that harder: run away, run through traffic, change direction twice, or start
already moving.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots 2003 and 2019 — Ty Law, Stephon Gilmore and the man-coverage habit"}
Two Patriots seasons, sixteen years apart, bookend Belichick's man-coverage defenses. In the 2003
AFC Championship Game against Indianapolis, Ty Law intercepted Peyton Manning three times in a
24–14 win, playing press-man against the Colts' receivers and, in his words afterward, the
simplest game plan imaginable: "Just beat them up." The rules response that followed, the 2004
crackdown on illegal contact, became known as the "Ty Law Rule."[^lawfilm]

In 2019 the Patriots led the NFL in points allowed (14.1 per game) and total defense, and Stephon
Gilmore became the first Patriot to be named Defensive Player of the Year, tying for the league
lead with six interceptions and returning two of them for touchdowns.[^gilmore] That was the
season New England led the league in man coverage (the talent paragraph above has the number),
and the habit around Gilmore was the Belichick one: man coverage on most of the field, and the
spare defenders spent on whatever the opponent most wanted to do, often its best receiver or tight
end.

**What to notice:** on a 2019 Patriots third down, find the free defenders first: usually a
safety deep in the middle and a second defender in the hole or bracketing the offense's best
receiver. The pattern repeats from 2003 to 2019 with different players: man coverage on the people
the defense trusts, and the free defenders spent on the player or the area it fears.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs, Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024) — Spagnuolo brings the house"}
Overtime, 49ers ball, third-and-4 at the Kansas City 9. San Francisco called what looked like a
well-designed play-action pass for Jauan Jennings, and the replays later showed receivers coming
open. It didn't matter.
Steve Spagnuolo sent six rushers in Cover 0, Chris Jones came through untouched, and Brock Purdy
had to let the ball go early; it sailed over Jennings's head. San Francisco settled for a field goal, and Patrick
Mahomes answered with the game-winning touchdown drive. "On third down," linebacker Nick Bolton
said afterward, "we brought the house." "They brought Zero," Purdy said.[^sb58]

**What to notice:** an all-out pressure on a third down inside the 10 is the Cover 0 bargain at its
most favourable for the defense. The field is short, so the deep ball that punishes Cover 0
everywhere else barely exists; the throw has to be quick anyway; and one free rusher is enough to
end the play. Watch for the same ingredients on any Chiefs third down near the goal line: the
safeties walking down, everyone pressed, and a count of rushers that exceeds the count of
blockers.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Jets at Raiders, December 6, 2020 — the bargain lost"}
The other side of the bargain. The winless Jets led the Raiders 28–24 with seconds left, and Las
Vegas was near midfield. Defensive coordinator Gregg Williams called an all-out blitz with Cover 0
behind it. Derek Carr stood in and threw deep, and Henry Ruggs ran past his rookie cornerback,
one-on-one with nobody behind him, for a 46-yard touchdown with 5 seconds left: Raiders 31,
Jets 28. The Jets fired Williams the next day.[^jets]

**What to notice:** everything that makes Cover 0 a good bet at the goal line makes it a bad one
here. The field was long, so the deep ball existed; the offense needed a big play, not a few
yards; and one lost footrace decided the game. Compare it with the Super Bowl LVIII snap above:
same call, opposite situation.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Jets 2009 — the shadow"}
Watch any 2009 Jets game against a team with a star receiver and follow Darrelle Revis before the
snap. When the star moves from one side to the other, Revis moves with him, and the other Jets
defenders reshuffle around that one fixed matchup. (Denver's 2024 opener at Seattle, with Surtain
on Metcalf, shows the same thing in the modern game.)

**What to notice:** the shadow corner's matchup frees the rest of the defense. Against Revis's
receiver the Jets often needed no help at all, so the safety who would have bracketed him was
available to rob, blitz or double someone else. That is what a shadow corner is really worth: one
player doing the job of two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday"}
**Who's facing the quarterback?** It is the fastest man-or-zone test there is.

- **Before the snap: the corners.** Squared up to the receiver, close, weight forward, eyes on the
  receiver's belt: lean man. Turned inside, deeper, eyes on the quarterback: lean zone.
- **Before the snap: motion.** Does somebody run across the formation with the man in motion?
  That is man. Do the defenders shift over and swap? Could be either: watch the next clue.
- **Before the snap: the safeties.** One deep safety in the middle and corners pressed: think
  Cover 1. *Nobody* deep and six or seven players on or near the line on third down or near the goal
  line: think Cover 0 and expect a quick throw.
- **At the snap: the eyes.** One second after the snap, look at the defenders underneath. Backs
  turned to the quarterback, running with receivers: man. Facing the quarterback, settling into
  areas: zone. The one defender in the middle facing the quarterback when everyone else is
  running with someone is the rat or robber. Find him and you'll know where *not* to throw.
- **Close formations.** When receivers stack or bunch, watch the two or three defenders over them
  at the release. Do they cross each other (locked man) or trade (banjo)?
- **The star.** Where is the offense's best receiver, and who is on him? The same corner every
  snap, on both sides of the field, is a shadow. A safety 10 to 12 yards deep and only a few
  yards inside him, far from the middle, is a bracket.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the man in the middle"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-robber .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread(rb_w=-2.0)
off = [q.moved(w=7.0) if q.key == "H" else q for q in off]
off = [q.moved(w=11.5) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
dfn = cover1_def(extra={"NB": (3.5, 7.6), "SS": (10.6, 3.4), "MIKE": (4.8, 11.0), "WILL": (4.5, -1.6),
                        "LCB": (1.2, -15.9), "RCB": (1.2, 15.9)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=8)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
branch(fld, p, [(-1.5, -9.0), (-2.8, -6.0), (-2.8, 4.5), (-1.6, 6.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(4.0, -9.8), (3.0, -6.0), (3.0, 4.6), (3.4, 6.4)], lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 6.4, -6.5, "$ followed H across", fontsize=6.6)
number(fld, p, [("Z", "#1"), ("Y", "#2"), ("H", "#3")])
field_legend(fld.ax, ["motion", "react", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

Before the snap, H motioned from the left slot across to the right (blue dashes) and the nickel ($) ran across with him (orange dashes); both are shown where they finished, so the offense is now 3x1 to the right (Z, the tight end Y, and H, who is now #3). The corners are pressed, a step outside. One safety (FS) is 14 yards deep in the middle; the other (SS, ringed) stands 10 yards deep, just off the middle.](06-02-man-coverage_files/figure-html/fig-predict-robber-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-robber}
:::
:::


**What coverage is this most likely to be, and which throw should the quarterback avoid? What
would you call to beat it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 1 with a robber.** The tells stack up: the nickel *travelled* with H's motion all the way
across the formation, which is man coverage; the corners are pressed and squared up; and there is
exactly one safety deep in the middle, so the middle of the field is closed. Now count. Five
receivers need five men: two corners, the nickel on H, the Mike on the tight end, the Will on the
back. That leaves the second safety, 10 yards deep near the middle, with nobody to cover. He is the
free defender, a robber, and his job is to read the trips side and the quarterback and jump the
first route that breaks into the middle.

**Avoid** the single in-breaking route into his area: a lone dig or crosser at 8 to 12 yards is
exactly the throw he is there to steal, as in the robber animation earlier in the chapter.
**Attack** him with a high-low: a shallow crosser underneath and a dig behind it (the drive
concept), so he can't take both, or look him off to the middle and throw outside. You could also
attack the corners one-on-one away from the robber with a back-shoulder fade or a double move,
since the free safety must cover the whole deep middle, or put the running back on a linebacker
with an angle route.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: who has the back?"}

::: {#cell-fig-predict-zero .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread(rb_w=2.0)
dfn = zero_front() + [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.4, -9.6, "$"),
                      D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 10.0, 1.2, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=80, to_go=6)
p.highlight("FS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
branch(fld, p, [(9.2, 1.2), (7.8, 1.2)], lw=1.2)
say(fld, p, 11.6, 7.4, "creeping\nforward", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["react", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Third-and-6 at the defense's 30. The offense has 11 personnel in a 2x2: four receivers spread out and the running back (R) beside the quarterback. The corners and the nickel are pressed on X, Z and H, and the strong safety is 4 yards off the tight end Y. Six defenders are on the line, including both linebackers in the A gaps beside the center. The only other defender is the free safety (FS, ringed), 10 yards deep in the middle of the field, creeping forward as the quarterback calls the signals.](06-02-man-coverage_files/figure-html/fig-predict-zero-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-zero}
:::
:::


**Count it. If all six defenders on the line rush, who covers the running back? So what coverage
is coming, and what should the offense do about it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 0, with a six-man rush.** Five receivers need five men. Four of them are already standing
on their receivers: two corners, the nickel, and the strong safety on Y. The fifth man is the
only one left, the free safety, and he is the only possible cover man for the running back. That
is why he is at 10 yards and creeping rather than at 13 to 15: he isn't guarding the deep middle,
he is getting closer to *his man*. So nobody will be deep, and six rush. (Compare Predict the play 1,
where there were *two* players beyond the linebackers and the arithmetic left one free.)

Could it still be Cover 1? Only if one of the six on the line drops out to take the back and the
free safety stays deep; a defense can also show this and drop players out at the snap (the
"simulated" pressures of
[Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).
But a lone safety at 10 yards, creeping, on third down, is the classic picture of zero.

**What the offense should do:** count the rushers against the blockers. Six rushers against five
linemen means one comes free, so the back should stay in to block. That makes it six against six,
and if the free safety then joins the rush ("hug"), the quarterback must throw hot, now, to a
receiver winning against an inside-shaded defender: a quick out, a fade, or a rub. And because
nobody is deep, any receiver who wins a vertical route is a touchdown.
:::
:::

::: {#cell-fig-predict-bracket .cell execution_count=18}

``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread(rb_w=-2.0)
dfn = cover1_def(extra={"MIKE": (4.0, 7.8), "WILL": (4.5, -2.0), "SS": (10.0, 7.5), "FS": (14.0, -1.0),
                        "NB": (1.4, -9.6)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=7)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

![Third-and-7. The offense's best receiver is its tight end, Y, in the right slot of a 2x2. The Mike (M) is 4 yards off him, shaded inside. The strong safety (SS, ringed) is 10 yards deep, a step and a half inside Y. The free safety (FS) is 14 yards deep in the middle. The corners and the nickel are pressed on X, Z and H; the Will (W) is over the running back.](06-02-man-coverage_files/figure-html/fig-predict-bracket-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-bracket}
:::
:::


**What are the two defenders over Y doing, and where should the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 1 with a bracket on the tight end.** Count: four rushers, and five receivers with a man
each (the corners on X and Z, the nickel on H, the Will on the back, the Mike on Y). That leaves two
spare defenders. One, the free safety, is deep in the middle: Cover 1. The other, the strong
safety, has nobody to cover and yet stands only a step and a half inside Y, 10 yards deep, which
no robber would do (a robber sits in the middle). He is the "over" half of an under-over bracket on
Y, and the Mike, tight and inside, is the "under" half.

**Throw somewhere else.** The bracket's bill is paid in the middle: with the strong safety spent on
Y, nobody sits in the hole. A crosser from H or X has room once it clears the Mike's area, and the
running back on the Will (an angle route) is a classic answer. X and Z are one-on-one with only the
free safety behind them. Throwing to Y into two defenders on third-and-7 is what the defense is
daring the quarterback to do. A defense can disguise this, of course, by standing the safety there
and playing something else; and the same lean against a 3x1 formation can also belong to a
split-field coverage check (see
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Man coverage covers people, not places.** It is tight, certain about who covers whom, and lets
  the defense pick matchups. Its price is that man defenders watch receivers, not the
  quarterback, and need help somewhere.
- **The free defenders define the family.** Cover 1 keeps one safety deep and usually one more
  defender to rush, rob or spy; Cover 0 keeps nobody deep and usually sends six or seven. The rat, the robber
  and the lurker are the same idea: one defender with zone eyes, in the middle, where man coverage
  is weakest.
- **Leverage follows the help.** With inside help (Cover 1), corners usually play outside and
  funnel receivers inside (split, down and distance can change it); with no help (Cover 0), they
  play inside and protect the quick throw.
  Technique (press, off, trail) is chosen per matchup and per down.
- **Close formations and great receivers get special rules.** Banjo and combo calls stop stacks
  and bunches from creating rubs; brackets spend two defenders on one star; a shadow corner spends
  one.
- **Man coverage is a situational weapon.** In the charted NFL seasons it was most common on third
  and short-to-medium and near the goal line (where Cover 0 is often the most common call), and
  least common on third-and-long. The public man-rate trend breaks at 2022/2023 because the
  charting source changed.
- **Every man-beater makes staying with a receiver harder:** crossers and mesh, rubs, slants
  against leverage, double moves, motion at the snap, a back on a linebacker, a scrambling
  quarterback. The defense's counters are the free defender, the banjo and the bracket.
